items.plain: Feeling leads to perception, perception to thinking, and thinking to mental proliferation. That runaway proliferation is where the judgments that trouble a person come from.
items.core_idea: Runaway thinking breeds the judgments that trouble us.

items.plain: Whatever a mendicant keeps thinking about becomes the way their heart leans. Dwell often on sensual thoughts and you drop renunciation, and the mind bends toward sensuality.
items.core_idea: What you dwell on shapes your heart.

items.plain: The Buddha recalls that when a sensual thought arose in meditation, he saw that it harms oneself, others and both, blocks wisdom and leads away from freedom. Seeing this, the thought faded, and he let all such thoughts go.
items.core_idea: Seeing a thought's harm makes it fall away.

items.plain: When a mendicant's focus stirs up thoughts of desire, hate or delusion, they should switch to a wholesome subject. The bad thoughts end and the mind settles, like a mason knocking out a large peg with a finer one.
items.core_idea: Replace unwholesome thoughts with wholesome ones.

items.plain: Others may criticise you kindly or harshly, truly or falsely, lovingly or with hidden hate. However it comes, the Buddha tells mendicants to keep their minds steady, speak no bad words, and spread love to that person and the world.
items.core_idea: Meet any criticism with steady, boundless love.

items.plain: A caretaker of a sal grove cuts out crooked saplings and tends the straight ones, and the grove grows. Likewise, mendicants should drop the unwholesome and devote themselves to the wholesome, and they will grow in this teaching.
items.core_idea: Remove the unwholesome and tend the wholesome to grow.

items.plain: Even if bandits were sawing you limb from limb, anyone who felt hatred because of it would not be following the Buddha's teaching. Instead, keep the mind steady and spread love to them and to the whole world.
items.core_idea: Hold love even toward those who torture you.

items.plain: Asked whether people can feel anxiety over what isn't outwardly there, the Buddha says yes: when someone mourns what was once theirs or what they can't get, they grieve, wail and fall into confusion.
items.core_idea: Grieving what's lost or unattained creates anxiety.

items.plain: When others abuse you, don't become resentful and bitter; when they honour you, don't become elated. If they praise you, simply think that it's for something already understood long ago.
items.core_idea: Stay unmoved by both abuse and praise.

items.plain: There are two quests, noble and ignoble. The ignoble quest is when someone who will be reborn, age, sicken, die and grieve goes looking for things that are subject to all the same.
items.core_idea: Seeking perishable things while perishable is the ignoble quest.

items.plain: Before his awakening, the Buddha says, he too chased things that age, sicken and die, as he did himself. Then he asked why he didn't instead seek what is free of all that: extinguishment, the supreme sanctuary.
items.core_idea: Seek what is beyond aging and death.

items.plain: The spiritual life isn't lived for possessions, honour, popularity, or even for ethics, meditation or insight. Its goal, core and final end is an unshakable freedom of heart.
items.core_idea: Unshakable freedom of heart is the spiritual life's goal.

items.plain: A monk tells the Buddha how lucky he feels to live with such companions. He treats them kindly in deed, word and thought, and sets aside his own ideas for theirs; though different in body, they are one in mind.
items.core_idea: Kindness and yielding make companions one in mind.

items.plain: A person developed in body and mind feels pleasure without craving it and pain without wailing or falling apart. Neither pleasant nor painful feelings take over their mind.
items.core_idea: A developed mind is not seized by pleasure or pain.

items.plain: A mendicant is content with robes for the body and almsfood for the belly, taking only these wherever they go, like a bird whose only burden is its wings. Living ethically, they feel a blameless inner happiness.
items.core_idea: Travel light, like a bird with only wings.

items.plain: Mendicants might think that having conscience and prudence is enough and the work is done. The Buddha warns them: while there is still more to do, don't lose sight of the goal.
items.core_idea: Don't settle early while more remains to do.

items.plain: We won't overeat. We'll eat thoughtfully, not for fun or looks, but only to keep the body going, avoid harm and support practice, ending old discomfort without creating new.
items.core_idea: Eat mindfully, only to sustain body and practice.

items.plain: Anyone, from any direction, can quench their thirst at a cool lotus pond. Likewise, anyone of any class who comes to the Buddha's teaching and develops love, compassion, rejoicing and equanimity finds inner peace, which is true ascetic practice.
items.core_idea: Inner peace is open to anyone, whatever their origin.

items.plain: Asked what the body must lose before it lies discarded like a senseless log, the answer is three things: vitality, warmth and consciousness.
items.core_idea: Without life, warmth and consciousness, the body is a log.

items.plain: Pleasant feeling is pleasant while it lasts and painful when it ends; painful feeling is the reverse. Neutral feeling is pleasant when you understand it and painful when you don't.
items.core_idea: Every feeling turns into its opposite when it passes.

items.plain: There are four ways of taking up practices: pleasant now with future pain, painful now with future pain, painful now with future pleasure, and pleasant now with future pleasure.
items.core_idea: Practices differ in present and future pleasure or pain.

items.plain: Beings generally wish that unpleasant things would shrink and pleasant things grow. But exactly the opposite happens to them.
items.core_idea: We wish for more pleasure, yet get the opposite.

items.plain: The Buddha asks quarrelling mendicants whether wounding each other with barbed words is treating each other kindly. They admit it isn't, and he warns that such behaviour will bring them lasting harm and suffering.
items.core_idea: Quarrelling with cutting words brings lasting harm.

items.plain: A baby quickly pulls back a hand that touches a burning coal. In the same way, someone with right view who slips into a fixable offence quickly confesses it to the Teacher or a wise companion and restrains themselves afterward.
items.core_idea: The wise quickly confess and correct their faults.

items.plain: A fire doesn't plan to burn the fool, yet the fool who attacks it gets burned anyway.
items.core_idea: Attacking what is pure only harms the attacker.

items.plain: There are four kinds of people: those who torment themselves, those who torment others, those who do both, and those who do neither. The last live without cravings in this life, cooled, blissful, become divine.
items.core_idea: Harming neither self nor others leads to bliss.

items.plain: A noble disciple eats in moderation by reflecting that food is not for fun or looks, but only to sustain the body, avoid harm and support spiritual practice, ending old discomfort without creating new.
items.core_idea: Eat in moderation, only to sustain the practice.

items.plain: A man parades through town in a borrowed carriage and jewels, and people think he's rich. When the owners take back their things, he has reason to be upset, because none of it was ever his.
items.core_idea: Borrowed pleasures can be taken back at any time.

items.plain: The Buddha tells a householder to act only after careful thought, especially since he is well known.
items.core_idea: Act only after careful consideration.

items.plain: Showing Rāhula a little water left in a pot, the Buddha says that's how little of the ascetic's nature remains in those who aren't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie.
items.core_idea: Shameless lying empties out the spiritual life.

items.plain: The Buddha asks Rāhula what a mirror is for; it's for checking your reflection. In the same way, every deed of body, speech and mind should be done only after checking it again and again.
items.core_idea: Check every action as you would a mirror.

items.plain: After acting, check whether the deed harmed yourself or others. If it did, confess it to the Teacher or a wise companion and hold back in future. If it didn't, live in joy and keep training in what is good.
items.core_idea: Review your deeds: confess harm, rejoice in good.

items.plain: The Buddha tells Rāhula to meditate like the earth. People throw clean and filthy things on it, yet it isn't disgusted; meditating this way, pleasant and unpleasant experiences won't take over his mind.
items.core_idea: Be like the earth, unmoved by clean or foul.

items.plain: Meditate on love and ill will falls away; on compassion and cruelty falls away; on rejoicing and discontent falls away; on equanimity and aversion falls away.
items.core_idea: Each wholesome meditation removes its opposite.

items.plain: A man struck by a poisoned arrow refuses treatment until he learns who shot him, the man's looks and home, and every detail of the bow and arrow. He would die before learning any of it.
items.core_idea: Demanding every answer first can cost your life.

items.plain: When a horse trainer first gets a fine thoroughbred used to the bit, it twists and dodges because it is new to this. But with regular, gradual practice its bad behaviour fades away.
items.core_idea: Gradual, steady practice tames resistance.

items.plain: A very poor man envies a calm meditating monk and wishes he could go forth. Yet he can't give up even his broken hovel, couch, grain pot and wife, though none is anything special.
items.core_idea: Even poor attachments can bind us strongly.

items.plain: Enlightenment isn't achieved all at once but by gradual training and practice. Someone with faith approaches a teacher, listens, remembers and examines the teachings, strives, and finally sees the ultimate truth with wisdom.
items.core_idea: Enlightenment comes through gradual training.

items.plain: Greed is unwholesome and contentment wholesome; hate is unwholesome and love wholesome; delusion is unwholesome and understanding wholesome.
items.core_idea: Contentment, love and understanding overcome greed, hate, delusion.

items.plain: Arguing leads to dispute, dispute to distress, and distress to harm.
items.core_idea: Arguments lead step by step to harm.

items.plain: All feelings, whether pleasant, painful or neutral, are impermanent and arise from conditions; they are bound to end, vanish and fade away.
items.core_idea: Every feeling is impermanent and passes.

items.plain: The Buddha sees beings consumed and burning with craving for sensual pleasure, and doesn't envy them. He knows a satisfaction apart from sensual pleasure that rivals heavenly joy, so he has no wish for the lesser kind.
items.core_idea: A higher joy frees you from envying sensual pleasure.

items.plain: A leper scratches his sores and scorches them over coals; the wounds only get worse, yet he finds some relief in it. Likewise, the more people indulge sensual pleasure, the more their craving burns, though they still find some gratification.
items.core_idea: Indulging craving feeds it, like scratching a wound.

items.plain: Health is the greatest blessing, and extinguishment the greatest happiness.
items.core_idea: Health is the best blessing; extinguishment the best happiness.

items.plain: The senses give sensual pleasure, but beyond it lies a pleasure that rises above the sensual, and that is said to be the best.
items.core_idea: A pleasure beyond the senses is the best.

items.plain: A baby swaddled up to the neck is released from those wrappings as it grows and its senses mature. It knows it is free, and there are no more bonds.
items.core_idea: Growing maturity releases us from our bonds.

items.plain: Four summaries of the teaching: the world is unstable and swept away; it has no shelter or saviour; it has no owner, and you must leave it all behind; it is always wanting, a slave to craving.
items.core_idea: The world is unstable, unprotected, unowned and craving.

items.plain: Family and friends can't help you as you die; wealth, children and kingdom stay behind, and beings go on by their deeds. Life is short for all, but only the fool is struck down; the attentive don't tremble.
items.core_idea: Death takes everything; only the wise stay unshaken.

items.plain: The Buddha saw that his extreme self-torment, as severe as anyone's, hadn't brought awakening. Then he remembered entering a blissful first absorption as a boy under a plum tree, and realised that this was the path to awakening.
items.core_idea: Awakening came through gentle absorption, not self-torment.

items.plain: The Buddha saw that beings differ: some have little dust in their eyes, some much; some are easy to teach, some hard. Like lotuses, some stay underwater, some reach the surface, and some rise clear of the water.
items.core_idea: Beings differ in readiness, like lotuses in a pond.

items.plain: The killer Aṅgulimāla asks how the walking Buddha has stopped while he hasn't. The Buddha answers that he has stopped forever by laying aside violence toward all creatures, but Aṅgulimāla can't stop harming living beings.
items.core_idea: True stopping means giving up all violence.

items.plain: Someone who was once careless but became careful, whose bad deeds are replaced by good ones, lights up the world like the moon freed from clouds.
items.core_idea: Turning from bad to good makes a person shine.

items.plain: Irrigators guide water, fletchers straighten arrows and carpenters straighten timber, but the wise tame themselves.
items.core_idea: The wise shape themselves.

items.plain: You can have full faith in something and it may still be empty and false. And you can lack full faith in something and it may still be true.
items.core_idea: Strong faith doesn't make something true.

items.plain: Striving helps you arrive at the truth. Without striving you won't get there; you reach the truth because you strive.
items.core_idea: You reach the truth by striving.

items.plain: The Buddha says he doesn't tell people to serve everyone, nor no one. Don't serve someone if serving them makes you worse; do serve someone if serving them makes you better.
items.core_idea: Serve those whose service makes you better.

items.plain: The Buddha says that being born into an eminent family, being very beautiful, or being very wealthy does not make you a better or worse person.
items.core_idea: Birth, beauty and wealth don't make you better.

items.plain: There are ways of earning a living that are both profitable and honest. With them you can support your parents, avoid bad deeds and follow the path of goodness.
items.core_idea: Honest work can support family and goodness.

items.plain: You are not a brahmin or a non-brahmin by birth. Your deeds make you a brahmin, and your deeds make you a non-brahmin.
items.core_idea: Your deeds, not your birth, define you.

items.plain: There are five hindrances: sensual desire, ill will, dullness and drowsiness, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
items.core_idea: Five hindrances block the mind.

items.plain: A man struck by a poisoned arrow has a surgeon cut, probe, extract and cauterise, each step sharply painful. In time the wound heals, and he is healthy, happy, independent and free to go where he likes.
items.core_idea: Painful treatment can lead to lasting health.

items.plain: A mendicant sees that living as they please makes bad qualities grow, while striving hard makes good ones grow, so they strive. Later they no longer need to strive hard, because they have reached the goal they strove for.
items.core_idea: Hard effort is needed only until the goal is reached.

items.plain: If you see that correcting someone would trouble you and hurt them, because they're irritable and stubbornly cling to their views, and you can't turn them toward good, don't underestimate the value of equanimity toward them.
items.core_idea: With some people, equanimity is the wise response.

items.plain: A bronze goblet holds a drink with lovely colour, smell and taste, but it is poisoned. Would someone who wants to live and be happy drink it, knowing it would bring death or deadly suffering?
items.core_idea: Don't drink pleasure you know is poisoned.

items.plain: Sensual pleasures are impermanent, hollow, false and deceptive. They are made of illusion, and only fools are taken in by them.
items.core_idea: Sensual pleasures are hollow illusions.

items.plain: Out of compassion the Buddha has done what a caring teacher should. He points Ānanda to the tree roots and empty huts and urges him to meditate, not to be negligent, and not to regret it later.
items.core_idea: The teacher has shown the way; now practise.

items.plain: The Buddha tells a mendicant to eat in moderation, reflecting that food is not for fun or looks but only to sustain the body, avoid harm and support practice, ending old discomfort without creating new.
items.core_idea: Eat in moderation, only to sustain the practice.

items.plain: The Buddha didn't praise every kind of meditation. He didn't praise meditating while secretly gripped by desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness or doubt, without understanding how to escape them, and just brooding.
items.core_idea: Meditation that hides inner hindrances isn't praised.

items.plain: A true person gives advice that doesn't hurt themselves, others or both.
items.core_idea: Good counsel harms no one.

items.plain: A true person gives carefully, with their own hand and with thought. They don't give leftovers, and they consider the consequences of their gift.
items.core_idea: Give carefully, personally, and thoughtfully.

items.plain: A true person knows that fame doesn't end greed, hate or delusion; anyone who practises the teaching properly deserves honour, famous or not. So they keep their practice to themselves and don't use fame to raise themselves and belittle others.
items.core_idea: Practice, not fame, makes a person worthy.

items.plain: All dangers, perils and hazards come from fools, not from the wise. It's like a fire that starts in a grass hut and burns down even a well-built, sealed house.
items.core_idea: Danger comes from fools, not the wise.

items.plain: Whoever develops mindfulness of the body includes every wholesome quality that leads to realisation, just as picturing the ocean includes all the streams that flow into it.
items.core_idea: Mindfulness of the body contains all the good.

items.plain: A mendicant who loves company and groups doesn't shine and can't easily find the peace of renunciation, seclusion and awakening. One who lives alone, withdrawn from the group, can find these pleasures easily.
items.core_idea: Solitude, not company, brings deeper peace.

items.plain: The Buddha says there isn't a single sight that, when it decays and perishes, wouldn't bring sorrow, pain and distress to someone who desires it.
items.core_idea: Whatever we crave brings sorrow when it fades.

items.plain: The Buddha says he won't coddle his disciples like a potter handling damp, unfired pots. He will correct and push them again and again, and what is solid will stand the test.
items.core_idea: Hard correction reveals what is sound.

items.plain: Someone needing oil heaps sand in a bucket, sprinkles it with water and presses it, but gets no oil, whether they wish for it or not. That is simply the wrong way to get oil.
items.core_idea: The wrong method fails, whatever you wish.

items.plain: Those who keep repeating that someone abused, hit, beat or robbed them never lay their hatred to rest; those who let go of such grudges do. Hatred is never ended by hatred, only by love: this is an ancient teaching.
items.core_idea: Hatred ends not by hatred but by love.

items.plain: If you find a wise, attentive friend, travel with them joyfully and mindfully through every hardship. If not, walk alone like a tusker in the wild; there's no fellowship with fools. Better alone and doing no wrong.
items.core_idea: Better to walk alone than with fools.

items.plain: When a fool rests, their past bad deeds of body, speech and mind settle over them, like the shadow of a great mountain falling over the land in the evening.
items.core_idea: Past wrongdoing weighs on the fool like a shadow.

items.plain: Seeing that grasping is the source of birth and death, those who cling to nothing are freed from both. Happy and safe, at peace in this very life, they have moved beyond all hostility, fear and suffering.
items.core_idea: Letting go of grasping frees you from suffering.

items.plain: Don't run back to the past or reach for the future; the past is gone and the future hasn't come. See clearly what is here now. Work keenly today, for death may come tomorrow and can't be bargained with.
items.core_idea: Live fully in the present; death won't wait.

items.plain: Beings own their deeds and inherit them. Their deeds are their origin, their family and their refuge, and it is deeds that make some beings lower and some higher.
items.core_idea: We are shaped by our deeds.

items.plain: Don't indulge in sensual pleasure, which is low and pointless, nor in self-torment, which is painful and pointless. Avoiding both extremes, the Buddha found the middle way, which leads to insight, peace, awakening and extinguishment.
items.core_idea: The middle way avoids indulgence and self-torment.

items.plain: Don't speak about people behind their backs, don't speak sharply to their faces, and don't speak in a rush.
items.core_idea: Speak openly, gently and unhurriedly.

items.plain: If what you'd say about someone, behind their back or sharply to their face, is false, don't say it. If true but useless, train yourself not to say it. If true and helpful, know the right time to say it.
items.core_idea: Speak only what is true, useful and timely.

items.plain: Speaking in a rush tires the body, stresses the mind and voice, makes the throat sore and makes words unclear. Speaking unhurriedly avoids all this, and your words are clear and easy to understand.
items.core_idea: Speak slowly to speak clearly and calmly.

items.plain: Don't neglect wisdom, keep to the truth, grow in generosity, and train only for peace.
items.core_idea: Wisdom, truth, generosity and peace.

items.plain: People are purified by their deeds, knowledge, principles, ethical conduct and right livelihood, not by family or wealth.
items.core_idea: Conduct, not family or wealth, purifies.

items.plain: Fellow monks plead with the gravely ill Channa not to take his own life. They want him to keep going, and promise to find him suitable food, medicine and a capable carer if he lacks them.
items.core_idea: Friends plead for a suffering companion to live.

items.plain: Time flies and nights slip by; the stages of life leave us one after another. Seeing the danger of death, do good deeds that will bring you joy.
items.core_idea: Life passes quickly; do good while you can.

items.plain: The monks don't grieve over the past or long for the future; they live on whatever each day brings, and so they look serene. Fools, longing for the future and grieving the past, wither like a cut green reed.
items.core_idea: Living in the present keeps you serene.

items.plain: Children bring you sorrow, and so do cattle. A person's attachments are their sorrow; without attachments there is no sorrow.
items.core_idea: Attachment is the source of sorrow.

items.plain: A mendicant should draw in their thoughts as a tortoise draws its limbs into its shell. Independent, disturbing no one, at peace, they blame no one.
items.core_idea: Gather your thoughts in, like a tortoise.

items.plain: If you think of yourself as equal to others, better or worse, you'll end up arguing over it.
items.core_idea: Comparing yourself with others breeds dispute.

items.plain: Whoever wrongs an innocent, pure person finds the harm turns back on them, like fine dust thrown into the wind.
items.core_idea: Wronging the innocent rebounds on you.

items.plain: You don't need to guard the mind against everything, even if it isn't yet fully controlled. It only needs guarding from where bad things come.
items.core_idea: Guard the mind only where harm enters.

items.plain: Keep company only with good people and stay close to them. Understanding the teaching of the good, you won't grieve among those who grieve.
items.core_idea: Keep good company and you won't grieve.

items.plain: When a miser holds back from giving out of fear, what they fear comes about anyway. The hunger and thirst they dread harm the fool in this world and the next.
items.core_idea: Stinginess brings the very want it fears.

items.plain: Those who share gladly from the little they have, like fellow travellers on a road, don't die among the dead. Some with little give happily while some with much won't give; a gift from little is multiplied a thousand times.
items.core_idea: Giving from little is worth a thousandfold.

items.plain: Gloom and suffering are both born of desire. Remove desire and gloom goes; remove gloom and suffering goes.
items.core_idea: Remove desire, and gloom and suffering go.

items.plain: Pretending to be someone you're not is like a cheating gambler enjoying stolen winnings. Say only what you will do, not what you won't; the wise can tell someone who talks without acting.
items.core_idea: Say only what you will actually do.

items.plain: If you refuse to forgive a mistake that has been confessed, holding hidden anger and hate, you stay trapped in enmity. The speaker doesn't approve of such enmity, and so forgives the mistake.
items.core_idea: Refusing to forgive keeps you trapped in enmity.

items.plain: Fools give themselves over to carelessness, but the wise guard their diligence as their greatest treasure.
items.core_idea: Diligence is the wise person's treasure.

items.plain: When your house burns, you save the useful pot, not the burnt one. The world burns with old age and death, so save by giving, since only what's given is saved. Enjoy what you have, and also give it away.
items.core_idea: What you give away is what you truly save.

items.plain: Kill anger and you sleep at ease, free of sorrow. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, for when it's gone there is no sorrow.
items.core_idea: Ending anger ends sorrow.

items.plain: There are six holes through which your wealth drains away: laziness, negligence, lack of initiative, lack of restraint, sleepiness and sloth. Get rid of them completely.
items.core_idea: Laziness and carelessness drain your wealth.

items.plain: A person shouldn't give themselves away or abandon themselves. Speak when your words are good, but not when they are bad.
items.core_idea: Don't abandon yourself; speak only good words.

items.plain: Kāmada complains that the path is rough and hard. The Buddha replies that the noble keep going anyway: the ignoble fall headlong on rough ground, but the noble find the path smooth, because they stay smooth amid the rough.
items.core_idea: The noble stay smooth on a rough path.

items.plain: A spirit asks the Buddha whether he feels delight; he asks what he has gained. Whether he feels sorrow; he asks what he has lost. So he neither delights nor sorrows, and he agrees.
items.core_idea: Without gain or loss, neither delight nor sorrow.

items.plain: Fools act as their own worst enemies, doing wicked deeds that bear bitter fruit. It's not good to do something you'll weep over later; it is good to do what gladdens you afterward, as its effect stays with you.
items.core_idea: Do only what you won't regret later.

items.plain: A cart driver who leaves a smooth highway for a rough road frets once his axle breaks. Likewise, a dullard who leaves the good for what opposes it frets when caught in the jaws of death.
items.core_idea: Abandoning the good leads to regret at death.

items.plain: When a forest is burned black by fire, new shoots still spring up there again as the days and nights pass.
items.core_idea: New growth returns even after fire.

items.plain: Kings' fine chariots wear out, and this body grows old too. But the teaching of the good never ages, as the good tell each other.
items.core_idea: Bodies age, but the truth of the good doesn't.

items.plain: People who do bad things in deed, word or thought don't really love themselves, even if they say they do, because they treat themselves like an enemy.
items.core_idea: Doing wrong is treating yourself as an enemy.

items.plain: If you truly held yourself dear, you wouldn't tie yourself to wrongdoing, because happiness is hard to find for someone who does bad deeds.
items.core_idea: Loving yourself means avoiding wrongdoing.

items.plain: When death seizes you, what is truly yours, and what goes with you like a shadow? Only the good and bad you have done in this life; that is what you take with you.
items.core_idea: Only our deeds go with us at death.

items.plain: Restraint of body, speech and mind is good; restraint everywhere is good. A sincere person who is restrained in every way is said to be protected.
items.core_idea: Restraint in all things protects you.

items.plain: Searching every direction with the mind, you find no one dearer than yourself. Others hold themselves just as dear, so someone seeking self-knowledge would harm no one.
items.core_idea: Everyone holds themselves dear, so harm no one.

items.plain: You can't know a person by looks, so don't trust them at first sight. Undisciplined people pass as disciplined, like a clay earring or a gilded copper coin: corrupt inside, beautiful outside.
items.core_idea: Appearances can hide corruption.

items.plain: A person who is always mindful and eats in moderation finds their discomfort easing; they age slowly and look after their life.
items.core_idea: Mindful, moderate eating eases and lengthens life.

items.plain: A killer breeds a killer, a conqueror a conqueror, an abuser abuse and a bully a bully. As deeds play out, the plunderer ends up plundered.
items.core_idea: What you do to others comes back to you.

items.plain: Like cool water in a deserted place that dries up undrunk, a bad person who gains wealth neither enjoys it nor gives it away.
items.core_idea: Hoarded wealth is wasted, like undrunk water.

items.plain: All beings are bound to die; death is their end and none is exempt. Just as every pot a potter makes, fired or unfired, will break, so all beings will die.
items.core_idea: All beings must die, as all pots break.

items.plain: Like huge mountains of rock closing in from every side, old age and death advance on all beings, high and low, crushing everything. No army, diplomacy or wealth can stop them.
items.core_idea: Old age and death crush everyone alike.

items.plain: The Buddha tells Māra that children and cattle bring sorrow. A person's attachments are their sorrow; without attachments there is no sorrow.
items.core_idea: Attachment is the source of sorrow.

items.plain: Days and nights rush past, and then life is cut short. Mortal life drains away like the water in tiny streams.
items.core_idea: Life drains away quickly.

items.plain: Even if you shook the whole of Vulture's Peak, those who are truly freed and awakened would not be shaken.
items.core_idea: The awakened cannot be shaken.

items.plain: Even people with a dart in the heart get some sleep, so why not the Buddha, whose dart is drawn out? He lies down unafraid and untroubled, sees no decline for himself, and is full of kindness for all beings.
items.core_idea: With the dart removed, one rests in peace and kindness.

items.plain: Let us live very happily, owning nothing. We will feed on joy, like the radiant gods.
items.core_idea: Owning nothing, we can live on joy.

items.plain: Take a mountain of pure gold and double it, and it still wouldn't be enough for one person. Knowing this, live a moral life.
items.core_idea: No amount of wealth satisfies; live morally.

items.plain: Once someone has seen where suffering comes from, how could they lean toward sensual pleasures? Seeing attachment as a chain in the world, they would train to remove it.
items.core_idea: Seeing attachment as a chain, remove it.

items.plain: The nun Somā asks what difference being a woman makes when the mind is serene and knowledge is present as she rightly sees the Dhamma.
items.core_idea: Being a woman is no bar to wisdom.

items.plain: Everyone is born with an axe in their mouth, and fools cut themselves with it by saying bad things. Praising the blameworthy or blaming the praiseworthy is a losing hand you deal yourself; it never brings happiness.
items.core_idea: Careless words wound the one who speaks them.

items.plain: All conditioned things fall apart. Keep going with diligence.
items.core_idea: Everything passes; persist diligently.

items.plain: Conditioned things are impermanent; their nature is to arise and pass away. Having arisen, they cease, and their coming to rest is true bliss.
items.core_idea: The stilling of all that arises is bliss.

items.plain: Kill anger and you sleep at ease, free of sorrow. Anger has a poisonous root and a sweet tip; the noble ones praise destroying it, for when it's gone there is no sorrow.
items.core_idea: Ending anger ends sorrow.

items.plain: Getting angry at an angry person only makes things worse for you; not getting angry wins a hard battle. If you stay mindful and calm when someone is angry, you act for both your good and theirs.
items.core_idea: Staying calm with an angry person helps you both.

items.plain: The fool thinks they've won when they use harsh words. But for someone who understands, patient endurance is the real victory.
items.core_idea: Patient endurance, not harsh words, is victory.

items.plain: Asked who can untangle people tangled inside and out, the Buddha answers: a wise mendicant grounded in ethics, developing mind and wisdom, keen and alert, can untangle this tangle.
items.core_idea: Ethics, meditation and wisdom untangle the tangle.

items.plain: Don't ask about someone's birth; ask about their conduct, for fire can be born from any sticks. A steady sage, even from a low-class family, is a thoroughbred restrained by conscience.
items.core_idea: Judge people by conduct, not birth.

items.plain: The Buddha tells a fire-worshipping brahmin that conceit is his burden, anger his smoke and lies his ashes. The tongue is the ladle, the heart the fireplace, and a well-tamed self is a person's true light.
items.core_idea: A well-tamed self is your true light.

items.plain: The Buddha describes his farming: faith is his seed, effort his rain, wisdom his yoke and plough, conscience and mindfulness his tools. He guards body and speech, eats moderately, cuts with truth and finds release in gentleness.
items.core_idea: Spiritual practice is a kind of farming.

items.plain: An old father laments that the sons he rejoiced over drove him out at their wives' urging. Calling him dear Dad, they proved monsters, and now, like an old horse led from its feed, he begs at others' homes.
items.core_idea: An aged father is cast out by his sons.

items.plain: Someone who loves to contradict, whose mind is tainted and aggressive, can't understand fine words. Once you let go of aggression, suspicion and resentment, you'll understand them.
items.core_idea: Let go of hostility to understand wise words.

items.plain: The Buddha has nothing to do in the jungle: his own inner jungle is cut at the root and withered. Free of its snarls and thorns, he enjoys solitude, having given up discontent.
items.core_idea: With the inner jungle cleared, solitude is joy.

items.plain: A monk sees it as his own misfortune that lust has left him dissatisfied. How could anyone else end his discontent and bring him satisfaction? He decides to do it himself.
items.core_idea: Only you can dispel your own discontent.

items.plain: Everything that has form, on earth, in the sky or deep below, wears out; all of it is impermanent. Those who examine themselves live having understood this.
items.core_idea: All that has form wears out.

items.plain: A man begs Ānanda to tell him how to quench his burning lust. Ānanda answers that his mind is on fire because of distorted perception; he should turn away from the attractive features of things that stir lust.
items.core_idea: Lust burns from distorted perception.

items.plain: Speak only words that don't hurt yourself or harm others; that is well-spoken speech. Speak pleasing words, gladly welcomed, that bring nothing bad to others. Truth is undying speech, and the good say the teaching rests on truth.
items.core_idea: Speak truthful words that harm no one.

items.plain: A deity tells a monk who sought seclusion that his mind still strays outward. Let go of longing for people, stay mindful, don't let sensual dust drag you down; shake it off, as a bird shakes off dirt.
items.core_idea: Shake off worldly longing like a bird shakes off dust.

items.plain: A dedicated ascetic must put up with many sounds and shouldn't be dismayed, because sounds don't defile you. If you startle at every little noise like a deer in the woods, you'll be called flighty and your practice won't succeed.
items.core_idea: Don't be startled by every noise.

items.plain: You are consumed by your thoughts because you apply your mind irrationally. Give up that irrationality and make sure your thoughts are sound.
items.core_idea: Unwise attention lets thoughts consume you.

items.plain: Two voices describe the same moment: the still of high noon, birds settled, the great forest humming. One finds it frightening; the other finds it delightful.
items.core_idea: The same moment can frighten or delight.

items.plain: To someone without blemish who always seeks purity, even the tiniest bit of evil looks as big as a storm cloud.
items.core_idea: To the pure, small faults look huge.

items.plain: Things always go well for the mindful, and each day is better for them, yet they aren't free of enmity. But someone who delights in harmlessness day and night, loving all living beings, has enmity for no one.
items.core_idea: Love for all beings ends all enmity.

items.plain: Don't do bad deeds, openly or secretly. If you have done one or are doing one now, you won't escape suffering, even if you fly away and flee.
items.core_idea: You can't flee the results of bad deeds.

items.plain: A spirit urges Anāthapiṇḍika on: a hundred elephants, horses, chariots and a hundred thousand jewelled maidens aren't worth a sixteenth of one step forward. Go forward, householder, and don't turn back!
items.core_idea: One step forward outweighs great riches.

items.plain: One who is fully at peace always sleeps at ease. Sensual pleasures slip off them; they are cool and unattached. Having cut off all clinging and removed the heart's stress, the peaceful sleep well.
items.core_idea: Without clinging, you sleep in peace.

items.plain: Asked about the best wealth, happiness, taste and life, the Buddha answers: faith is the best wealth, the teaching practised well brings happiness, truth is the sweetest taste, and the best life is lived by wisdom.
items.core_idea: Faith, truth and wisdom make the best life.
